props.text: Your first call, in about ten minutes

The Arcline Platform is a REST API organised around resources. Everything accepts and returns JSON, everything is authenticated with an OAuth 2.0 bearer token, and everything is rate-limited per token.

items: An Arcline account with API access enabled — **Settings → API keys → Generate**.
Node.js 20 or later, or Python 3.11 or later. Official SDKs exist for both.
Outbound network access to api.arcline.example on port 443, TLS 1.3.
A working knowledge of REST, OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and webhook delivery.

props.text: Requests reach a single gateway, which terminates TLS, applies rate limits and validates the bearer token before routing to one of three internal services. Events travel the other way.

props.text: **Figure 1.** Request path, authentication path and event path. Everything your integration touches is behind the single gateway host.
Three environments, each with its own credentials. A token issued for one is rejected by the others.
Sandbox resets every Sunday at 00:00 UTC. Do not build fixtures that assume data survives it.
Install the SDK, take credentials from the environment, and list the first page of users.
One call proves the chain: credentials, token exchange, TLS, routing and scopes.

items: **200** — everything works; the body carries the API version and region.
**401** — the token is wrong, expired, or issued for another environment.
**403** — the token is valid but carries no scope at all.
**Timeout** — egress is blocked; check the firewall before anything else.

props.text: Tokens, scopes and the refresh you do not have to write
Every request carries a bearer token obtained through the OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow. Tokens expire after 3,600 seconds; the SDKs refresh them for you, sixty seconds early.

**Never ship a client secret to a browser.** The client credentials flow is for server-to-server calls. For browser and mobile clients, mint a short-lived scoped token on your own backend and hand that out instead.

props.text: **Figure 2.** The client credentials exchange, end to end.

POST https://auth.arcline.example/oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant\_type=client\_credentials
&client\_id=YOUR\_CLIENT\_ID
&client\_secret=YOUR\_CLIENT\_SECRET
&scope=users:read users:write events:subscribe
Send the token on every subsequent request in the Authorization header.
Scopes are requested at token exchange and cannot be widened afterwards. Ask for the narrowest set the integration needs; a token that can only read is a token that can only leak reads.

items: Store client secrets in a secret manager, never in source control or an image layer.
Keep tokens in memory. Writing one to disk or to a log turns a 60-minute window into an incident.
Rotate client secrets every 90 days; the platform accepts both the old and the new secret for 24 hours after a rotation.
Request one scope set per integration rather than one shared admin token for all of them.
Revoke immediately at Settings → API keys if a secret is exposed; revocation takes effect within 30 seconds.

props.text: Nine resource families, one operation vocabulary. Learn the shape once and every endpoint behaves the way you expect.

props.text: Every list endpoint is cursor-paginated. Offsets are not supported: a cursor is stable across inserts, and an offset is not.
Pass next_cursor back as the cursor query parameter to fetch the following page. A response with has_more set to false is the last page, and next_cursor is then null.
Limits are applied per token, in a sliding 60-second window. Every response carries the current state in its headers, so a well-behaved client never needs to be told twice.

props.text: Webhooks push state changes to an endpoint you own, within seconds. Every delivery is signed, and every delivery is retried until you acknowledge it or the platform gives up.

props.text: Every delivery uses the same envelope. The event-specific body sits under data.

Verify the X-Arcline-Signature header before you trust a payload. It is an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body, keyed with your endpoint secret. Compare it in constant time — a plain equality check leaks the answer one byte at a time.
**Verify against the raw body.** Signing happens before parsing, so a body that has been through a JSON round trip will not match — key order and whitespace both change the hash.
A delivery counts as failed on any non-2xx response, or on no response within 30 seconds. Failed deliveries are retried on an exponential schedule.
After the fifth failure the event is marked failed and an alert is raised in the console. Failed events stay replayable for 30 days from **Settings → Webhooks → Delivery log**.
What the API says when it says no
Standard HTTP status codes, and one error body shape for all of them. The request_id in every error is what support will ask for first.

props.text: Network failures make it impossible to know whether a write landed. Send an Idempotency-Key header on every POST and PATCH and the question stops mattering: a replayed request returns the original response rather than creating a second resource.

props.text: **Generate the key before the first attempt, not inside the retry loop.** A key generated per attempt is a key that never matches, which is the same as having no key at all.
Not every failure deserves a retry, and the ones that do deserve a considered one. The rule is the status code: retry what the platform admits is its own fault, and fix what it says is yours.

props.text: Both SDKs log the full request and response, headers included. Never leave it on in production: the Authorization header is logged verbatim.
A ticket that arrives with these five things is usually answered in one round trip.

items: The request id from the error body.
The environment and base URL you called, verbatim.
The timestamp in UTC, and whether the failure is intermittent.
The scopes on the token, read from the exchange response.
One request and one response, headers included, token redacted.

props.text: What changes, and what never will
A version in the path is a promise: v3 keeps accepting the requests it accepts today. This page says how far that promise reaches, and where to go for everything this guide does not cover.

The version is in the path. v3 will keep accepting the requests it accepts today: new fields may appear in responses, and new optional parameters may be added, but nothing that works now will stop working inside a major version.

props.text: **Pin the version, not the host.** Calling the unversioned host follows whatever is current, which is exactly the upgrade you did not schedule.
